definition: In historical psychology and philosophy of mind, conscious automatism refers to a view in which bodily or physical events form an unbroken causal sequence, while conscious events accompany them without acting back on the body. In the source, it is treated as closely related to psychophysical parallelism and near a guarded form of materialism.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Double Aspect Theory; pinned source text

reasons: The packet’s entry is for “Double Aspect Theory,” not a definition of “conscious automatism” itself; it only says the theory may approximate that doctrine.

The specific wording that bodily or physical events form an unbroken causal sequence while conscious events accompany them without acting back on the body is not directly stated as the definition of conscious automatism in the packet.

The claim that the source treats it as closely related to psychophysical parallelism and near a guarded form of materialism is only partially supported and is tied to the double-aspect theory’s relation to conscious automatism, not to a standalone definition of the term.
